title: The same NQ strategy made 96% starting in 2016 and lost money starting in 2022
author: person-person12
selftext:
Same strategy, same 15 minute NQ candles, same all session rules, a 20 candle breakout with an ATR stop and target. The only thing I changed between these two runs is the date I told it to start from. The 15 minute NQ history in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) goes back to May 2016, so I ran it from the beginning of the data and then ran it again from January 2022.

**July 2016 to March 2026:** +95.8%, 6,119 trades, 38.9% win rate, profit factor 1.04, max drawdown 34.9%  
**January 2022 to October 2026:** -4.8%, 3,029 trades, 36.9% win rate, profit factor 1.00, max drawdown 63.8%

The second window is the one most people would reach for. Four and a half years feels like plenty of data, it is more recent, and it covers the market most of us actually remember trading. On that window the strategy earns nothing and gives back **63.8% of the account** at its worst point, against 34.9% on the long run.

**\_\_\_\_**

The number doing the damage is the profit factor. 1.04 on the long run means that across 6,119 trades it made a dollar and four cents for every dollar it lost. Sitting that close to the line, the thing has no real say in its own result, and the window gets to decide instead. Move the start date and the same rules print +96% or -5%.

Its the same reason a player's season average and any random five games off his schedule tell you two different things about him. The five games are real, every shot in them happened, and theyre still not the player.

What Id check on anything of my own before believing a number: how far the profit factor actually sits above 1, and whether I picked the start date for a reason or because thats where the data I had happened to begin. **3,029 of those trades sit inside both runs**, so the whole disagreement is one strategy being asked the same question twice.

comments.author: Alphanet_dogwalker
comments.body: are the end dates a typo? The first run ends in March and the second in October, so you're changing both ends of the test. i'd line those up first. Otherwise the extra months could explain part of the difference you're attributing to the start date.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Not a typo but **youre right that it was sloppy**, the 2016 run ended 03-31 and the 2022 one ended 10-01, so six extra months were riding along with the start date change.

I lined them up and reran the 2022 one to 03-31. It came in at -2.52% instead of -4.81%, against +95.8% for the run that starts in 2016. So the extra months were worth about two points and the start date is still carrying the rest of it.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Good catch on the end dates. Fixing both runs to the same end and then only changing the start is the cleanest way to attribute the gap to the start date, and extending the second window back to March 2026 for comparison would show how much the extra months matter.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: A cleaner way to show this is a rolling start: run the same rules from every month-start in the data to the same end date, and plot the distribution of final returns. That turns “+96% or -5%” into a spread, so you can see how much of the result depends on the start. It also helps to split the 6,119 trades by year, since the 3,090 trades that only sit in the long run (2016 to 2021) must carry all of the profit, and with a profit factor of 1.04 and 1.00 the strategy itself isn’t doing much in either window. Cymetica’s Backtest Labs is one place to see how strategy results get compared against a benchmark.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: The rolling start is the right way to show it, agreed. Every month start run to the same end date gives you a spread instead of two dates I picked, and Ill run it that way. The profit factor is the bigger tell though, 1.04 and 1.00 means the start date argument is really about which side of breakeven the noise lands on.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Agreed, with a profit factor that close to 1, the start date mostly decides which side of breakeven you land on. When you run the spread, a quick number to add is the share of start months that finished positive, because that shows how fragile the result is in one figure.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Thats a better single number than the spread is, agreed. Rolling every start month and counting the share that finished positive is one run, so ill add it to the next one. Do you cap each window at 12 months or let them all run to the end?

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: I'd run both and report them separately, because they answer different questions. Fixed 12-month windows show what a typical year looks like and give you many comparable samples, while letting every start run to the same end date shows what happens if you started on a bad month and stayed in. If you only do one, the 12-month cap is easier to read, but then the windows overlap heavily, so I'd keep the sample count honest and call it roughly the number of non-overlapping years, not the number of start months.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: The overlap point is the one that actually bites. **A hundred and twenty monthly starts across ten years of history is ten independent years wearing a bigger number**, and calling it 120 samples makes the spread look better measured than it is. Fixed 12 month windows for the typical year, and one run from each start through to the same end date for the stuck-in-it case, reported apart so nobody reads one as the other.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That plan covers it. One extra check when you report the stuck-in-it runs: also show the worst start month, not only the share that finished positive, since the loss from the unluckiest start is the number people feel most. Thanks for the clear exchange.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Fair, the worst start is the number that actually costs somebody money, so ill put it in beside the share that finished positive. Its the same set of runs either way.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Sounds good, that covers it. I'll leave it there, thanks for the clear exchange.
